items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Oh, we had to call Klook to come in from Japan, Klook who was a notorious

ctx.x: What do you do as a promoter?

Well, you feel badly for the Japanese promoters, but you still have buddies (Rich and Louie Belson and Philly Jo, and Charlie Persip) who are in jail. And you go to the Japanese jail and you say, "Why can't you let these guys out on bail? You're hurting your own thing. They pay bail and come back and stand trial or you can deport them, or whatever you want to do." "No way!" So you hire a Japanese drummer, you know, who's the Japanese Gene Krupa, they call him, and ... the next year I wasn't in Japan but it…

items.title: 52031_Kenny Clarke oral history interview
items.q: Because George Wein, I knew him when he was in school, in high school

ctx.x: And that's what it springs from.

You see? Now, then, they told me, he says, "That's all right. You'll never work in New York again." So I began to calculate, I said, "Oh, yeah, I guess I'm washed up there." It's still going on today. Because George Wein, I knew him when he was in school, in high school, because his brother -- I worked at a club, his brother was manager, at the [Kitten] Club in Boston, and George, he was about 15 or 16 years old, was still going to high school. But the message got out about Kenny is a troublemaker. So Norman…
